scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is a high school senior asking if she's the asshole for refusing to cook dinner for her mom while schools are closed online. 

First, I need to understand the dynamics here. The key points:
- Mom works outside home (6-minute commute, finishes at 5pm)
- Dad works demanding job (home earliest 6pm, often 9-10pm)
- Dad is the skilled cook who actually prepares meals
- Mom "refuses to learn" cooking, consistently makes "low effort flavourless meals" or doesn't cook at all
- Dad has been compensating by cooking late or eating fast food before home
- User and younger sister have been doing schoolwork online
- User cooked during first 3 weeks of closure but now refuses due homework load
- Mom expects them to cook "because we're home all day" despite school assignments
- User's argument: "we're home all day but not free all day"
- Dad ended up cooking today

Hmm... this is clearly a family role imbalance. Let me mentally list who's doing what:
- Mom: works outside home, but doesn't cook, watches TV, "s sits on her ass" (user's words)
- Dad: high demanding job, still does all chores, cooks, compensates for mom's lack
- User: high school senior with online school workload, previously helped with cooking but now overwhelmed
- Younger sister: also in school, presumably same workload

The core issue seems to be mom's expectation that "being home all day" = free time for chores, while ignoring that schoolwork is real work. 

*Pausing to consider cultural context*... in some households, "home all day" might imply " free for domestic duties," but that's not how modern education works. Online school requires focused time - it's not like being "home from school" with no responsibilities. 

Looking deeper at the power dynamics:
- Dad is doing all the heavy lifting (work + chores + cooking)
- Mom is not contributing meaningfully to household tasks
- User is being asked to take on cooking duties while juggling schoolwork, which is unfair given:
  - Mom's own cooking skills are poor (user says " awful cook")
  - Dad is capable and willing to cook
  - User has already been helping

*Checking for red flags*... 
- Mom's " ashamed of us and how we're useless" is emotionally manipulative language
- "S sits on her ass watching TV" - that's a strong description, but if true, it's a pattern of behavior
- Dad's " offers to cook for us" shows he's aware of the imbalance

*What would Jewish values say?*... 
- " * Tzedakah* " ( justice) - this situation lacks fairness in labor distribution
- " * Kavod* " ( respect) - mom's " shame" comments are disrespectful to her children's actual work
- " * Tikkun olam* " ( repair the world) starts with fixing your own home - this family needs better role distribution

*Practical perspective*... 
- High school senior with online classes has academic responsibilities equivalent to a full-time job
- "Cooking dinner" is a significant time commitment ( planning, shopping, prep, cooking, cleanup)
- Mom's " it doesn't take that long" is dismissive - even simple meals take 30-60 mins
- Dad is the logical person to cook since he's home first (earliest 6pm vs mom's 5pm) and skilled

*The real AITA question*... 
- Is the user wrong for not cooking when:
  a) She has schoolwork
  b) Mom has no cooking skills
  c Dad is capable and willing
  d) Mom has been shirking responsibilities for years

... I think the answer is clearly " no, you're not the asshole." 

*Why?* 
- Mom's expectation is unreasonable given her own behavior ( she's not cooking, not learning, not sharing labor)
- Dad should be the primary cook since he's home first and skilled
- User's schoolwork is legitimate work - " home all day" doesn't mean " free for chores"
- Mom's " shame" comment is emotional abuse, not valid criticism

*Additional angles*... 
- This isn't about " being home all day" - it's about " being home with schoolwork" 
- The family's labor distribution is broken: 
  - Mom: work outside home + no domestic contribution
  - Dad: work outside home + all domestic work
  - Kids: schoolwork + expected to do extra chores
- Dad's " offers to cook for us" shows he knows this is unfair

*Final judgment*... 
- User is not AITA
- Mom is the one acting unreasonably by:
  - Expecting kids to cook while she's not contributing
  - Using " shame" as a manipulation tactic
  - Refusing to learn basic cooking skills
- Dad should step up more - he's the only one with both time and skill to handle meals

*What should happen next*... 
- Dad should take over cooking duties full-time
- Mom should either learn to cook or contribute in other ways (e.g., grocery shopping, cleanup)
- User and sister should focus on schoolwork - their " work" is academic, not domestic

*Why this isn't " being ungrateful"*... 
- User has been helping ( " did a lot of cooking during first 3 weeks")
- Now she's saying " I can't do this on top of schoolwork" - that's reasonable
- Mom's " you're useless" is completely out of proportion to " not cooking one dinner"

*TL;DR*... 
- User is not AITA
- Mom's expectations are unfair
- Dad should be cooking
- This is a family system problem, not the user's fault
- " AITA" framing is wrong - the real issue is mom's behavior and the family's unbalanced labor distribution

*Double-checking*... 
- No, I don't see any valid reason to blame the user
- If anything, the " asshole" is mom for her entitled attitude and lack of contribution
- Dad's complicity ( " ended up cooking") perpetuates the problem, but he's not the one being asked " AITA" here
